extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria for judging or composing lyric and narrative poetry, emphasizing imagery, diction, metre, character-representation, and the intellectual depth of the poet. Draws on examples from Shakespeare, Milton, and Romantic-era debates (Wordsworth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery moulds and colours itself to the circumstances, passion, or character, present and foremost in the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery should adapt to and arise from the prevailing circumstances, passions, or character in the poet's mind; fitting the psychological and situational context of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge points to unrivalled instances in Shakespeare (LEAR, OTHELLO, sonnets) as models. Imagery that is characteristic to the feeling and situation (not generic ornament) demonstrates poetic genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery that conveys succession with the feeling of simultaneousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's imagery should be able to represent a sequence of events while giving the reader a vivid sense of them occurring together or immediately felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example lines cited: 'With this, he breaketh from the sweet embrace... homeward through the dark laund runs apace' and 'Look! how a bright star shooteth from the sky, So glides he in the night from Venus’ eye.' Such imagery fuses movement and instantaneous perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet must possess intellectual depth and energetic thought; poetry is the blossom of extensive human knowledge and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘No man was ever yet a great poet, without being at the same time a profound philosopher.’ Coleridge emphasizes that creative power must be accompanied by intellectual energy — study, meditation, broad knowledge — as seen in Shakespeare's combination of imaginative force and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as student: study, meditation, and deliberate knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic genius is not merely spontaneous inspiration; the poet must study patiently, meditate deeply, and acquire knowledge so that it becomes habitual and intuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge opposes the idea of the poet as a passive vehicle of inspiration; he praises poets who 'first studied patiently, meditated deeply, understood minutely.' This is presented as necessary for lasting poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect dominion/mastery over the whole world of language
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should command language fully — a wide and sovereign command of words, phrases, and registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge remarks on Shakespeare's 'perfect dominion, often domination, over the whole world of language' as part of his greatness; mastery enables variety and appropriateness across characters and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between striking/new imagery and careful diction & metre
rubrics_metrics.description: While novel and striking images are valuable, they must be paired with careful, principled diction and metrical construction rather than careless or purely convenient forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge criticizes contemporary poets who pursue new images and specific portraiture but are 'comparatively careless' in diction and metre. Metre should acknowledge a justifying principle, not merely the writer's convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: plain sense, genuine native English, and avoidance of meretricious finery
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction should favor plain sense and the genuine mother tongue over ornate, fashionable, or artificially learned expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Pope to Darwin some works illustrate the opposite vice. Coleridge applauds recent return to plainness in popular writers, warns against 'soiled and over-worn finery of the meretricious muse,' and invokes Dante's injunction to guard the purity of one's native tongue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superior excellence in the manner of treating familiar subjects (polish & simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should demonstrate mastery by treating common or traditional subjects with superior manner, exquisite polish of diction, and perfect simplicity rather than seeking novelty of subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge compares this to Italian and Flemish painting where foregrounds are made compelling; poets of fifteenth/sixteenth centuries aimed for 'exquisite polish' and harmonious metrical movement rather than novelty of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and harmony achieved through subtle modification of native metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety in metrical movement should be achieved by countless subtle modifications and balances within the common metres of the language, not by adopting mechanically dominant foreign metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge criticizes the introduction of new foreign metres with overpowering mechanical tunes, preferring the older practice of nuanced variation within native metric forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding mere novelty for novelty's sake (clarity and logical diction over caprice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must avoid illogical, obscure, or arbitrarily novel diction intended only to surprise; such language substitutes 'folly and vanity' for good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet who indulges in 'arbitrary and capricious habits of expression' is criticized; clarity and intellectual coherence are preferred to transient wonder produced by novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of refined polish and vigorous insight (combine merits of older and modern poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal poet would unite the high finish, appropriateness, facility, delicate proportion, and pervasive grace of earlier masters with the keener interest, deeper pathos, and fresher imagery of moderns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge expresses a wish for a poet who combines the best qualities of both eras (e.g., Catullus/Anacreon polish + modern depth and variety of imagery). This is a prescriptive ideal for poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as essentially ideal and generic; characters should be representative of a class
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be 'essentially ideal': its individualities must be representative (generic) attributes of a class, not mere accidental traits of one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoking Aristotle, Coleridge argues persons in poetry must be clothed with common attributes of their class to serve the purposes of poetry; this limits how far literal, singular details should govern poetic characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and adaptation of rustic language (do not adopt rustic speech wholesale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of low and rustic life, even if purified of provincialisms, is not automatically the best poetic diction; rustic speech must be adapted, reconstructed, and often supplemented with reflective vocabulary for poetic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge disputes Wordsworth's claim that the 'real language of men' (rustics) is the proper poetic medium. He argues that rustic vocabulary is limited and must be corrected to conform to grammar and to express general/abstract relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid literal imitation of dull or garrulous speech in lyric or poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In lyric and many forms of poetry, faithfully imitating dull or garrulous speech reproduces tedium; the poet should avoid unmitigated imitation that drags the poem's tone down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge notes that in 'The Thorn' and similar pieces an introductory context was needed to justify a narrator's credulous garrulity; in lyric poems especially, mimicry of dullness risks unpleasant 'sinkings' from prior poetic height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide necessary context when using dialect or eccentric narrator voice
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poem uses dialect, provincialisms, or an idiosyncratic narrator, the poet should supply prior context or framing to prevent misreading and to make the representation plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wordsworth ought to have prefaced 'The Thorn' with a poem portraying the speaker's character to prevent readers from interpreting the poem as mere stupidity or grotesqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language for poetry is largely derived from reflection on mental acts, not only from objects of rustic life
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valuable part of human language for poetry is that which expresses internal acts, imagination, and abstract relations; it is formed by reflection and education rather than solely by familiarity with natural objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues that much of the best poetic vocabulary comes from philosophical and reflective discourse (e.g., Bible, Liturgy, learned prose), and that rustic experience alone yields a too-limited vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard the purity of the native tongue; avoid unnecessary learnedness or provincial corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should protect the native language's purity: avoid provincialisms and excessive pedantry, but also not substitute artificial or learned phrases that alienate naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge cites Dante and others in support of jealously guarding native diction; balance is required — neither meretricious ornament nor pedantic ostentation is acceptable.
